newsitem.title: UK: British interest rates unchanged, output fragile.
newsitem.headline: British interest rates unchanged, output fragile.

text.p: The Bank of England made clear Thursday that interest rates had been left unchanged at 6 percent as official figures showed manufacturing output was enjoying only a fragile recovery.
The central bank made no formal statement on monetary policy but it conducted money market operations at established dealing rates.

That provided definitive evidence that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, the finance minister, had ordered no change in rates Wednesday after his monthly monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
There had been a lingering suspicion on financial markets that a rate rise might be announced Thursday.

George, who fears a resurgence in inflation in the next 18 months, has been pressing for higher rates since December. But Clarke is anxious to avoid tightening monetary policy in advance of approaching national elections because it would mean higher home mortgage rates for millions of Britons.

Economists said December industrial production figures -- which both officials would have been aware of at their meeting Wednesday -- strengthened Clarke's argument that there was little immediate risk of the economy overheating.

Manufacturing output grew just 0.2 percent in December from the previous month after an unexpected 0.3 percent fall in November. The annual rate of growth accelerated to 1.4 percent from 0.5 percent in November.
Overall industrial production rose 0.6 percent in December and was up 1.9 percent year-on-year.
Economists said total industrial production was slightly stronger than expected in December, largely due to sharp rises in energy output because of unusually cold weather.
There was also robust growth in durable goods production, reflecting strong demand in the consumer sector.
"Overall, these figures provide confirmation that, while the manufacturing recovery remains on track, it is still fragile," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
Simon Briscoe, an economist at Nikko Europe, said the weakness in manufacturing was a strong argument for a stable monetary policy.

"We believe that the fragile state of the manufacturing sector probably provides enough ammunition for the Chancellor to keep interest rates on hold until after the election," he said. An election must be held by May 22.
